summaries.summary: Clinical summarization is essential in medicine, with handoff summaries, progress notes, oral case presentations, and discharge summaries supporting communication and coordinated care.
Poor quality clinical summaries, limited EHR functionality, fragmented data, dictation readability issues, and incomplete discharge summaries can cause communication failures and medical errors.
Automated summary generation may save clinician time, avoid medical errors, and aid decisions; this work assesses extractive summarization upper bounds and develops an HPI topic classifier.
Summarization methods progressed from frequency-based sentence extraction to topic modeling, cue word dictionaries, title methods, and recent sequence-to-sequence abstractive approaches.
EHR summarization approaches have largely been extractive and indicative, with few deployments, limited demonstrated outcomes impact, and no known neural network literature.
MIMIC-III contains deidentified ICU EHRs from Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center between 2001 and 2012, including 55,177 discharge reports and 4,475 addendums for 41,127 patients.
The first aim determines the upper bound of extractive summarization because discharge summaries may contain information discussed but never documented elsewhere in the EHR.
Discharge summaries were compared with current admission and entire record notes using UMLS CUIs extracted by Apache cTAKES and filtered to remove subsumed CUIs.
CUI overlap was calculated separately for chief complaint, major surgical or invasive procedure, discharge medication, and history of present illness sections, plus recorded genders.
For each of 55,177 discharge summary reports, CUI recall was calculated for current admission notes and entire longitudinal records, with low recall suggesting undocumented information.
Table TABREF14 shows section recall, with procedure highest at 0.807 and all five section recalls much higher than overall recall in Table TABREF13.
The upper bound analysis suggests extractive summarization alone may not recreate discharge summaries, while imperfect cTAKES CUI labelling requires further work.
A classifier was developed for HPI topics using 515 manually annotated notes, with 40% labeled by clinicians, 60% by non-clinicians, and 10 labels.
The LSTM model, adopted from Dernoncourt et al, jointly classifies each HPI word using token embedding, contextual representation, label scoring, and label sequence optimization layers.
Lowercase italics denote scalars, lowercase bold denotes vectors, and uppercase italics denotes matrices in the following descriptions.
The token embedding layer combines pretrained word2vec word embeddings from MIMIC (v30) and discharge notes with learned character embeddings, exploring CBOW and skip gram models.
Each character in a word is mapped to an embedding and input into a bidirectional LSTM that outputs the word's character embedding.
The token embedding layer outputs vector e by concatenating word embedding t and character embedding c.
The contextual representation layer feeds word embeddings into a bi-directional LSTM and outputs concatenated hidden states for each HPI word.
The label scoring layer uses a fully connected neural network with one hidden layer to output scores for each of the 10 categories for each word.
The Label Sequence Optimization Layer uses a linear chain CRF to compute labeling sequence probability and find the highest probability sequence.
T is a transition matrix, and INLINEFORM1 and INLINEFORM2 are score vectors describing the cost of beginning or ending with a label.
The probability of a sequence of labels is calculated by applying a softmax layer.
Cross-entropy loss is the objective function, using the correct label sequence and probability calculated according to the CRF.

The model was evaluated on 515 annotated HPI notes split 70% train, 15% development, and 15% test, using Adam, learning rate = 0.001, decay = 0.9, dropout rate of 0.5, batch size = 20, 20 epochs, and early halting after 3 epochs.
The impact of character embeddings, pretrained w2v embeddings, and learned word embeddings was evaluated on the dev set, with the best model reported on the test set.

Table TABREF16 shows dev set results: discharge summary embeddings outperformed all MIMIC notes, CBOW outperformed skip gram, character embeddings increased performance by approximately 3%, and learned word embeddings achieved 0.886.
The Learned Word Embeddings model achieved accuracy of 0.88 and F1-Score of 0.876 on the test set, with demographics and patient movement highest and vitals/labs and medication history lowest.

Diagnosis history, patient movement, and procedure/results words were frequently labeled as symptoms/signs, with misclassifications possibly due to inconsistent manual labelling and needing further standardization.
Future work should examine mislabeled categories and alternative architectures, because word level prediction can assign multiple labels to phrases and phrase segmentation is difficult.
Supplementing LSTM word embeddings with CUIs may improve performance by combining contextual word information with explicit medical domain expertise.
The paper developed a CUI-based upper bound on extractive summarization and a NN architecture jointly classifying HPI words, achieving excellent performance on a small heterogeneous dataset.
The authors thank named annotators, Pete Szolovits for guidance and pretrained word embeddings, and Tristan Naumann for providing the MIMIC CUIs.
